slides.narration_text: The alignment chain gave us the logic of performance, evidence, practice, feedback, and retry. Now we make the criteria clear enough that two reviewers would judge the same work in the same way. A separate thread is communication: the learner needs four of five communication indicators. A distinct angle is safety: both safety checks must pass. The word AND is the design issue here. Rapport, warmth, or strong communication cannot compensate for a safety failure. If safety fails, the learner needs correction and another attempt, because the lesson has to protect the non-negotiable parts of performance.

slides.narration_text: We just chose evidence that can reveal a responsive move. Now we look at how feedback helps a learner improve before that evidence is collected. First, the attempt is vague: “We will follow up soon.” Then the specific feedback asks, “Who will act, and when?” That produces a better retry: “I will call Friday morning. Does that work for you?” The improvement is not magic; it comes from feedback that names an owner, time, and confirmation question. In your own lesson, ask where feedback arrives and where the learner gets to try again.

slides.narration_text: The feedback example gave us the small improvement loop. Next, we place that loop inside a whole lesson sequence so practice precedes final judgment. First, Prepare gives learners a private first decision. Then Model makes the conversation moves visible. Practice and retry let learners try with feedback before the Demonstrate phase asks for final conversation evidence. Finally, Assess and transfer extend the work into note practice, evidence, and application. The fifty-five-minute total belongs to Maya’s example, not to every project. slides.narration_text: The sequence tells us when learners prepare, practice, demonstrate, and transfer. Now modality asks what each participation condition makes possible. On one side, Live interaction supports real-time communication, immediate responsive teaching, and collaboration. On the other side, asynchronous work gives time to read and think, plan and reflect, and draft or create carefully. Compared with simply labeling something live or asynchronous, this is a design tradeoff. Now imagine a learner who needs more processing time. What would you change while preserving the same criteria? A defensible adjustment changes the participation condition, not the target capability.

rows.narration_text: The alignment chain gave us the logic of performance, evidence, practice, feedback, and retry. Now we make the criteria clear enough that two reviewers would judge the same work in the same way. A separate thread is communication: the learner needs four of five communication indicators.
